INTERESTS OF AMICI CURIAE1
Amici curiae are Ph.D. historians who study American history from the colonial era through the early
twentieth century. Amici’s works have been published
in peer-reviewed journals, law reviews, and university
press monographs and anthologies. They have authored in-depth scholarship on the history of firearms
and weapons regulation and the social and legal context of the eras most relevant to this case. Their works
have been cited by numerous courts. Several Amici
have served as expert witnesses on historical topics in
Second Amendment litigation. A complete list of
Amici appears in the Appendix.
Amici submit this brief to inform this Court’s evaluation of the historical record inquiry that is key in
Second Amendment jurisprudence—a sometimes “difficult” task. New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n, Inc.
v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1, 25 (2022). Amici’s knowledge and
expertise will assist the Court in this endeavor.
INTRODUCTION AND
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
This case asks whether state and local restrictions
on assault weapons—used to commit some of the
deadliest acts of civilian violence on American soil in
the last 50 years—are “consistent with the principles
that underpin our regulatory tradition,” United States
v. Rahimi, 602 U.S. 680, 692 (2024), especially as it

1 Amici certify pursuant to Rule 37.6 that no party or party’s
counsel authored this brief in whole or in part and that no person
or entity, apart from amici curiae and their counsel, made a monetary contribution intended to fund the preparation or submission of this brief.

2


existed around the ratification of the Second and
Fourteenth Amendments.
Assault weapons “are not the modern equivalents
of weapons that were commonly possessed and employed for self-preservation by your shopkeeper, or
your butcher, or your blacksmith up the road in colonial America.” Bianchi v. Brown, 111 F.4th 438, 452
(CA4 2024) (en banc). New research quantifies the
technological gulf, finding that a semiautomatic AR-
15 rifle can deliver more kinetic energy in a minute
than twenty-five Brown Bess muskets. See Darrell A.
H. Miller et al., Lethality and the Historical Principles
of Arms Regulation, 54 Pepp. L. Rev. __ (forthcoming),
at 27 tbl.3, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7525418. The “dramatic technological changes” that resulted in this unprecedented
killing power, and the mass violence enabled by assault weapons, have provoked “unprecedented societal concerns” that warrant “a more nuanced
approach.” Bruen, 597 U.S., at 27.
Our country has a longstanding tradition of restrictions on certain types of weaponry when their features made them especially dangerous. Importantly,
when the “proliferation” of such weapons led to concern over community violence, Bianchi, 111 F.4th, at
466, legislatures used their police power to enact restrictions on those particular weapons while leaving
available other means of self-defense. The laws enacted by Cook County and Connecticut’s democratically elected leaders thus follow a rich regulatory
tradition dating back to colonial America.
Three points about that tradition are particularly
relevant here.

3


First, any consideration of what early American
regulators did or did not do in the colonial and Founding eras must begin with the historical context. The
overwhelmingly rural society of the time possessed
single-shot, muzzle-loading firearms—firearms with a
fraction of the lethality of those at issue here. They
also inhabited a much simpler governmental culture.
Early American legislators met rarely and briefly and
undertook a far narrower range of work than their
modern counterparts. Nonetheless, early American
authorities prioritized the protection of public safety
and devoted regulatory attention to specific weapons
deemed especially dangerous to public safety. While
the repeating arms of the type Petitioners and their
Amici raise were not subject to targeted legislation in
the Founding era, that is because they were far too
rare and inconsequential to merit regulation.
Second, weapon-specific legislation became much
more common starting in the early nineteenth century. The development and mass production of portable and concealable lethal weapons prompted public
safety concerns in the quickly urbanizing nation. Legislators responded with a wave of weapon-specific regulation. For example, nearly all states enacted some
sort of restriction on Bowie knives—weapons in common use for legal purposes that also posed distinct
public safety risks. These laws emerged in the 1830s,
were in force in many states upon the ratification of
the Fourteenth Amendment, and continued to be
passed into the early twentieth century. While concealed-carry restrictions were the most common type
of regulation, some states enacted effective prohibitions on Bowie knives. Crucially, none of these Bowieknife provisions were overturned on constitutional

4


grounds. Moreover, during Reconstruction, governments restricted access to Winchester’s new repeating
rifle—a novel technology that threatened public safety
when Klansmen and their allies attempted to acquire
it. In sum, the regulatory wave that emerged in the
early nineteenth century set an enduring pattern:
technological change leading to societal concerns that
provoke restrictions.
Third and finally, that national regulatory tradition produced a robust response to the dramatic technological change and intense societal concerns
prompted by automatic and semiautomatic weapons
in the early twentieth century. Legislatures enacted
machine gun statutes and regulations starting in the
late 1920s, many of which remain in effect to this day.
In the decades since, legislatures have repeatedly refined machine-gun laws as the technology evolved.
Throughout American history, states and localities
have chosen varying policy responses to the problems
posed by particularly dangerous weapons that threatened the safety of their communities. They demonstrate that modern Connecticut and Cook County
restrictions on assault firearms are “part of an enduring American tradition of state regulation.” Bruen,
597 U.S., at 69.
ARGUMENT
I. Early American Weapons Regulation Must
Be Understood in Its Historical Context.
Petitioners and their Amici appear to contend that
the relative scarcity of weapons restrictions during
the Founding era invalidates future regulations. See
Pet. Br. 5–7, 46; NRA Br. 3–4, 10–14, 24–27, 30. But

5


any comparison between modern laws and the laws
early Americans did or did not enact must begin with
the historical context. Early American arms regulations reflected the dangers that contemporary weapons posed in their social context, not the outer limits
of legislators’ constitutional authority.
a. Early American Weapons Regulations
Reflected the Society and Arms Technology of the Times.
Society and firearms of the colonial and Founding
eras were vastly different from today. Those differences inevitably shaped the scope and character of
weapons regulation. Whereas about 80 percent of
Americans now live in urban areas, colonial- and
Founding-era America was overwhelmingly rural and
agrarian. Rural families made up nearly 95 percent of
the colonial population, compared to about 20 percent
today. See U.S. Census Bureau, Nation’s Urban and
Rural Populations Shift Following 2020 Census (Dec.
29, 2022), https://www.census.gov/newsroom/pressreleases/2022/urban-rural-populations.html; U.S.
Census Bureau, Historical Statistics of the United
States, Colonial Times to 1957, at 14 (1960).
In addition to use of firearms for hunting and pest
management, the ongoing projects of controlling slave
labor and dispossessing Indigenous people of land required high rates of white gun ownership. Tellingly,
the largest concentrations of guns evident in sampled
probate records from the period are found among the
large Southern slaveholders. See Expert Report and
Declaration of Kevin M. Sweeney ¶¶ 14–17, Nguyen v.
Bonta, No. 3:20-cv-02470 (S.D. Cal. 2023); Brian De-

6


Lay, The Myth of Continuity in American Gun Culture, 113 Calif. L. Rev. 1, 14 (2025); see also, e.g., 3
Statutes at Large of South Carolina  395 (1838) (1734
law requiring slave patrols to be armed).
Moreover, men in British colonial America also required arms for service in militias and continental
regiments, particularly during periods of inter-imperial warfare. See George D. Moller, American Military
Shoulder Arms, Volume I: Colonial and Revolutionary
War Arms 9–12 (2011); Kevin M. Sweeney, Firearms
Ownership and Militias in Seventeenth- and Eighteenth-Century England and America , in A Right to
Bear Arms? The Contested Role of History in Contemporary Debates on the Second Amendment  61, 75 tbl.
3.5 (Jennifer Tucker, Barton C. Hacker & Margaret
Vining eds., 2019) (comparing relatively low levels of
firearms ownership in Quaker colonies versus New
England and Chesapeake ones in seventeenth-century America). In short, boosting white male gun ownership was a far more pressing problem for early
American legislators than trying to protect society
against criminal misuse of guns.
Early American firearms technology was also
vastly different from today’s weaponry. Formal militaries used sturdy, large-caliber muskets with bayonets. Most civilians preferred lighter, relatively smallcaliber smoothbore long arms known as “fusils,” “fowlers,” or “trade guns.” Kevin M. Sweeney, Firearms,
Militias, and the Second Amendment , in The Second
Amendment on Trial: Critical Essays on District of Columbia v. Heller 310, 329–342 (Saul Cornell & Nathan
Kozuskanich eds., 2013). Smoothbore pistols circulated in smaller numbers, and rifles were common in

7


some areas of western settlement. Preferences depended on needs. Muskets were more formidable on
eighteenth-century battlefields but less practical on a
farm. Rifles had greater range but took longer to load
and therefore averaged one round a minute instead of
two or three. See Harold L. Peterson, Arms and Armor
in Colonial America, 1526-1783 , at 198 (1956); De
Witt Bailey, British Military Flintlock Rifles, 1740-
1840, 76 (2002).
But in comparison to the firearms available today,
all of these weapons were functionally similar. In general, the eighteenth century was “a century which saw
little change” before the “dramatic” changes in arms
technology and production that characterized the
nineteenth century. Peterson, Arms and Armor , at
221–22. With vanishingly few exceptions, single-shot,
muzzle-loading, smoothbore firearms were the guns
that preoccupied the Founding generation. Ibid.
These firearms could obviously be deadly to individual targets. But their slow rate of fire and comparative unreliability meant that none could equip a lone
shooter to kill numerous people at once. Thus, the
common firearm in 1791 was “not remotely as significant a policy concern in the late-eighteenth century as
it is today.” DeLay, The Myth of Continuity, at 15, 32;
see also Randolph Roth, Why Guns Are and Aren’t the
Problem: The Relationship Between Guns and Homicide in American History, in A Right to Bear Arms?, at
135, 139–140.

8


b. Authorities in Colonial- and Founding-Era America Regulated Weapons
in the Name of Public Safety.
Early American legislatures had neither the staff,
the administrative infrastructure, nor the information-gathering capabilities needed to implement a
regulatory regime comparable to the one we have today. See William E. Nelson, The Eighteenth-Century
Background of John Marshall’s Constitutional Jurisprudence, 76 Mich. L. Rev. 893, 920 (1978).
Nonetheless, authorities in the colonial and
Founding eras shared a conviction that governments
had extensive regulatory authority and a duty to protect the public. Colonial and early American governments regulated weapons through common law and
enacted hundreds of positive laws that directly or indirectly regulated weapons. Nearly all of these regulations were motivated by concerns for public safety
as defined by white authorities. They included regulations forbidding discharge or carry of weapons in particular times and places, storage of gunpowder, and
dispossession of weapons from classes of people.2
Although colonial and Founding-era legislatures
were practically limited in their capacity to enact
sweeping weapons regulations, they did so when faced

2 See, e.g., Robert J. Spitzer, Gun Law History in the United
States and Second Amendment Rights , 80 Law & Contemp.
Probs. 55, 59–60, 72–74, 78–80 (2017); Saul Cornell & Nathan
DeDino, A Well Regulated Right: The Early American Origins of
Gun Control , 73 Fordham L. Rev. 487, 510–15 (2004); Joseph
Blocher & Reva Siegel, Guided by History: Protecting the Public
Sphere from Weapons Threats Under Bruen, 98 N.Y.U. L. Rev.
1795, 1805–06 (2023).

9


with specific risks posed by particularly dangerous
weapons. They crafted regulations on carrying or
brandishing particular weapons, even while more general prohibitions on assault and affray existed. For example, against a backdrop of violent crimes committed
with weapons such as clubs, dirks, and daggers, East
Jersey in 1686 prohibited the concealed carrying of
“pocket pistol[s], skeines, stilladers, daggers or dirks,
or other unusual or unlawful weapons ….” An Act
Against Wearing Swords, ch. 9 (1686), reprinted in
The Grants, Concessions, and Original Constitutions
of the Province of New Jersey 289–90 (2d ed. 1881).
c. The Lack of 18th-Century Regulations
on Repeating Firearms Says Little
About the Scope of the Second Amendment at the Time of Its Ratification.
Petitioners and their Amici contend that a lack of
regulation of eighteenth-century repeating firearms
forecloses restrictions on assault weapons today. In so
doing, they obscure vital context. The repeating firearms they describe, see, e.g., Pet. Br. 6–7; NRA Br. 4,
10–14, 26; Buckeye Inst. Br. 4–8; Second Amendment
Law Ctr. Br. 18–19; Cato Inst. Br. 19–20, were experimental novelties and otherwise uncommon.
Although governments of the era desired reliable
repeating firearms, in North America, none “functioned well enough to become militarily and commercially significant before the nineteenth century.”
DeLay, The Myth of Continuity, at 24. Newspaper references to repeating weapons in the period characterized them as novelties that people might pay to see.
The Cookson repeater described by Petitioners’ Amici,
see NRA Br. 10–11; Second Amendment Law Ctr. Br.

10


19; Cato Inst. Br. 19–20, was expensive, unwieldy, often unsafe, and extremely rare in the colonies; a single
1756 advertisement is little evidence of its commercial
availability. See David S. Weaver & Brian Godwin,
John Cookson, Gunmaker, 19 Arms & Armour 43, 43–
63 (2022).
Similarly, the firearm that Joseph Belton demonstrated in Philadelphia in 1777 was far less significant
than Petitioners imply. See Pet. Br. 6. Its superimposed system of loading alternating charges of gunpowder and balls in a single barrel was the “most
discredited” of the early repeat-fire designs, because if
the charges went off all at once, the barrel would burst
in the shooter’s face. Lewis Winant, Firearms Curiosa
166 (1955). In the end, Congress declined to engage
Belton. See Kevin M. Sweeney, Brass Fusil, 131 Am.
Hist. Rev. 773, 773–776 (2026). Although gunmakers
continued to create and promote similar weapons, by
the early 1820s the “complexity, and inherent danger”
of the superimposed system led to its “wholesale abandonment.” Andrew J. B. Fagal, The Promise of American Repeating Weapons, 1791-1821 , Age of
Revolutions (Oct. 20, 2016), https://ageofrevolutions.com/2016/10/20/the-promise-of-american-repeating-weapons-1791-1821.
Nor is there evidence that the Girardoni air rifle,
see Pet. Br. 6; Buckeye Inst. Br. 7; NRA Br. 12, ever
reached commercial circulation. See DeLay, The Myth
of Continuity, at 29–30. Lewis and Clark carried a single specimen on their expedition to the Pacific, used to
impress Native Americans along the way. Frederick J.
Chiaventone, The Girandoni Air Rifle: The Lewis and

11


Clark Expedition’s Secret Weapon , 14 Military Heritage 66 (2013), https://warfarehistorynetwork.
com/article/lewis-and-clarks-girandoni-air-rifle.
In sum, the extreme rarity of repeating arms for
civilian use in the eighteenth century meant that
these weapons posed no special risk to the public.
Then, as now, governments are not “require[d] … to
regulate for problems that do not exist.” McCullen v.
Coakley, 573 U.S. 464, 481 (2014) (citations omitted).
Instead, they “respond when the ramifications of a
technological development become more apparent
over time.” Ocean State Tactical, LLC v. Rhode Island,
95 F.4th 38, 50 (CA1 2024); see also Bianchi, 111
F.4th, at 464.
II. Nineteenth-Century Legislatures Restricted Bowie Knives and Other Weapons—Arms in Common Use for Lawful
Purposes—Because of Their Distinctive
Dangers.
Arms technology underwent massive changes in
the nineteenth century. Unlike the eighteenth century’s flawed repeating firearms, those changes led to
reliable weapons that actually produced social consequences. Starting in the Jacksonian era, state and local legislatures began responding with new
regulations. Many targeted specific weapons—including the Bowie knife, which offers a salient analogue
for distilling the “principles that underpin our regulatory tradition.” Rahimi, 602 U.S., at 692. Reconstruction-era regulation of new repeating rifles used by the
Klan further illustrates that tradition at work.

12


a. Dramatic Technological Change and
New Social Problems Produced a National Wave of Weapon-Specific Regulation.
A new wave of regulations targeting particular
weapons began to emerge in the early nineteenth century. Rapid urbanization, population growth, and the
Industrial Revolution’s advances in metallurgy, machine tooling, and mass production coincided to bring
unprecedented changes in society’s relationship with
weapons. For example, the advent of percussion-cap
ignition and improvements in industrial production
made affordable, single-shot pistols a mass-consumer
item by the 1820s. By the 1830s, these advances
opened the way for mass production of reliable repeating pistols. Industrialization and the market revolution also made fighting knives and other familiar
weapons more commonly available and affordable.
“Americans scrambled to buy” these weapons,
which were portable, concealable, and “ideal for killing in the heat of the moment.” Bianchi, 111 F.4th, at
465 (quoting Roth, Why Guns Are and Aren’t the Problem, at 121). Combined with population booms and
rapid urbanization, the proliferation of weapons led to
increases in armed crime. From the U.S.-Mexican War
through Reconstruction, homicide rates increased
dramatically. The U.S. became the most murderous
affluent society in the world by far. See Randolph
Roth, Michael D. Maltz, & Douglas L. Eckberg,  Homicide Rates in the Old West , 42 W. Hist. Q. 173, 173–
195 (2011).
In response, legislatures across the country passed
the nation’s first raft of modern weapons regulations.

13


These regulations built on a colonial- and Foundingera legal tradition wherein individual rights were understood and exercised within an overarching commitment to the public peace and welfare. See generally
William J. Novak, The People’s Welfare: Law and Regulation in Nineteenth-Century America  19–50 (1996).
The new laws included restrictions on weapons as varied as billy clubs, slungshots, sand clubs, Bowie
knives, and pistols. See generally Robert J. Spitzer,
Understanding Gun Law History After Bruen: Moving
Forward by Looking Back , 51 Fordham Urb. L.J. 57,
87–102 (2023) (collecting examples). And they included restrictions on concealed carry of various weapons, both before and after the ratification of the
Fourteenth Amendment.3 See Spitzer, Gun Law History in the United States, at 63–64 n.48 (collecting historical statutes).
b. Bowie Knife Restrictions in the Early
and Mid-Nineteenth Century Serve as
an Apt Historical Reference for Understanding Second Amendment Principles.
The Second Circuit below and courts around the
nation addressing like cases have homed in on the robust set of antebellum laws restricting Bowie knives
as relevantly similar to modern restrictions on assault

3 As they had in the colonial era, legislatures also continued to
regulate trap guns, now being mass-produced for setting traps.

basic historical backdrop of nineteenth-century regulation, when possession bans of privately held weapons would have been difficult or impossible to enforce.
While nineteenth-century officials exercised broad

enforce restrictions on private possession of consumer

thus focused on public carry and point-of-sale, which

III. The Regulatory Response to Automatic
and Semi-Automatic Fire Fits Squarely
into the American Tradition of Weapons
Regulation.
The pattern of socially consequential new weapons
technologies prompting regulation continued into the
early twentieth century with the spread of automatic
and semi-automatic firearms. As these novel weapons
generated societal concerns, legislatures adopted possession bans, permit regimes, and registration requirements. Some of those laws regulated both fully-
and semi-automatic firearms.
a. The Development of Automatic and
Semi-Automatic Fire Revolutionized
Firearms and Prompted Regulation.
Contrary to claims of gradual technological progress advanced by Petitioners’ Amici, see NRA Br. 6–
24; Buckeye Inst. Br. 4; Second Amendment Law Ctr.
Br. 1–2, the advent of automatic and semi-automatic
firearms in the late nineteenth century represented a
revolution in firearms technology. The combined
breakthroughs that led to these new weapons dramatically increased the killing power of firearms.
Earlier repeating firearms such as lever-action or
pump-action rifles and revolvers required energy
transferred from human muscle through an internal
mechanism to eject spent cartridges (or rotate them
out of the way) and then chamber a new round. When
all rounds had been fired, the shooter usually had to

27


reload bullet by bullet. These manual systems for cycling and reloading rounds limited rates of fire. Leveraction repeating firearms similar to the Winchester
1866 remain popular around the country today. Weapons restrictions, including magazine capacity laws,
nearly always include exceptions for “a tubular magazine that is contained in a lever-action firearm,” precisely because of their limited rates of fire. See Conn.
Gen. Stat. § 53-202w(a)(1)(C); Cook County, Ill., Code
of Ordinances § 54-211.
Automatic and semi-automatic firearms are different. They overcame stubborn rate-of-fire limitations,
thanks to the integration of three breakthrough technologies developed in the 1880s. First, Hiram Maxim
invented a reliable mechanism to capture the recoil
energy of a fired round to eject the spent casing and
chamber a new bullet. This could be done at speeds
that astonished the world—as many as 600 rounds a
minute. The Maxim Automatic Machine Gun Works ,
Scientific American, Oct. 9, 1886, at 225. Second,
French researchers perfected a chemical propellant
(“smokeless powder”) that was three times more powerful than traditional black powder, gave off little
smoke, and left behind almost no residue in the barrel.
That last quality was a prerequisite to sustaining high
rates of fire. See DeLay, The Myth of Continuity , at
44–46. Third, the development of detachable magazines enabled shooters to reload far faster than ever
before. Integrated together, these three innovations
drastically increased rates of fire and, therefore, killing power. See ibid.
The new automatic and semi-automatic firearms
first became commercially available in the late 1890s.

28


They grew more popular and varied through the early
twentieth century, including popular semi-automatic
pistols like the Colt M1911. See DeLay, The Myth of
Continuity, at 46 nn. 239–41; John Walter, The Hand
Gun Story: A Complete Illustrated History  127–44,
220–28 (2008).
However, some commercially available firearms
more resembled weapons of war. The most notorious
was the Thompson submachine gun—known colloquially as the Tommy Gun—introduced into the U.S.
market in the 1920s. Most models were select-fire,
meaning they could be set to automatic or semi-automatic modes. Many could be fitted with a drum holding up to one hundred rounds.  See Auto-Ordnance
Corp., Handbook of the Thompson Submachine Gun 3,
51 (1929).
Initially, the Thompson was available for sale at
hardware stores. As early as 1926, an influential reporter for Collier’s described the ease of ordering a
Tommy Gun from a Manhattan sporting-goods store,
arguing that the weapon “should be absolutely prohibited.” Owen P. White, Machine Guns for Sale , Collier’s, Dec. 4, 1926, at 11–12.
This sentiment soon became widespread, as criminals began using these weapons to kill people. Automatic weapons became notorious across the country,
associated with well-publicized murders and massacres. William J. Helmer, The Gun That Made the
Twenties Roar  102–28, 152 (1969). Bystanders were
caught in the crossfire. See, e.g., Child Is Killed; Four
Others Shot in Gang Warfare, Brunswick News (Ga.),
July 29, 1931, at 1. The most notorious incident took
place in Cook County, Illinois, when men associated

29

seven rivals in Chicago on Valentine’s Day, 1929. See

Chi. Daily Trib., Feb. 15, 1929, at 42.
As with the arrival of new weapons in the nineteenth century, the advent of automatic and semi-automatic fire prompted widespread societal concerns
and thus a new national wave of firearms regulation.

automatic firearms, and at least eighteen states,

The legislatures of the 1920s and 1930s, like lawmakers before them, restricted specific weapons that
posed a particular danger to the public. Now, they

specific firearms while leaving other weapons available for self-defense.
b. The Regulatory Tradition Has Iterated from the 1930s to the Present Day.
This Court has recognized that “dramatic technological changes” and “unprecedented societal concerns” may call for regulation that earlier generations
had no occasion to adopt. Bruen, 597 U.S., at 27. Congress’s response to the development and spread of automatic weapons shows how that has worked in
practice. Since the 1930s, legislatures have repeatedly
refined machine-gun laws as technology has evolved.
For example:
● In 1968, Congress extended the federal definition of “machinegun” to “any combination of

31


parts designed and intended for use in converting a weapon into a machinegun” after machine
gun conversion kits began to spread. Gun Control Act of 1968, Pub. L. No. 90-618, tit. II, 82
Stat. 1213, 1231; see 114 Cong. Rec. 10,862
(1968).
● In 1981, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and
Firearms classified the drop-in auto sear—a
small part that could convert some AR-15 pattern rifles to fully automatic fire—as a machine
gun. ATF Rul. 81-4, https://www.atf.gov/media/24261/download.
● And in 1986, Congress froze the civilian market
by prohibiting the transfer or possession of any
machine gun not lawfully possessed before enactment of the new law. Firearm Owners’ Protection Act, Pub. L. No. 99-308, § 102(9), 100
Stat. 449, 453 (1986) (codified at 18 U.S.C.
§ 922(o)).
Modern restrictions on assault weapons follow the
same sequence. These modern weapons derived from
military designs are far more capable of inflicting catastrophic injury than the deadly weapons of the
Founding. See Miller et al., Lethality, at 27–29. And
the line between these weapons and machine guns is
thinner than ever: today, “a semiautomatic rifle with
a bump stock can have the same lethal effect as a machinegun,” Garland v. Cargill, 602 U.S. 406, 429
(2024) (Alito, J., concurring), yielding rates of fire of
400 to 800 rounds per minute, Melissa A. Anderson &
Jonathan S. Jacobs, Garland v. Cargill and Machine
Gun Conversion Devices, 72 DOJ J. Fed. L. & Prac. 17,

32


18 (2024). Compared to the Brown Bess of the Revolutionary War, the discharge of kinetic energy in such
configurations is several hundred times greater. See
Miller et al., Lethality, at 27 tbl.3.12
These deadly advances in technology have produced a societal harm—mass shootings—that became
more prominent as those weapons proliferated. Modern legislatures responded by targeting the assault
weapons whose combination of features makes them
especially dangerous, while preserving numerous
weapons available for self-defense, just as historical
legislatures did to particularly dangerous weapons of
their day.
CONCLUSION
This Court should affirm the judgments below.
